tfn.s: The factory in Curitiba opened in July 2025.

focus.note: A collocation is a pair of words that naturally go together. Learn the pair as one piece, for example catch a disease.

focus.note: Verbs are picky about their nouns. You raise awareness, face criticism and measure results, but you do not do them the other way round.

tfn.s: The writer implies that insecticide has one advantage over the Wolbachia approach.
tfn.why: The text says spraying "at least offers visible, immediate reassurance".

tfn.s: The writer suggests that the Wolbachia approach removes the need for other disease-control measures.
tfn.why: The text says even successful programmes "must coexist with surveillance, treatment, sanitation" and the removal of breeding sites.

tfn.s: Residents were consulted before the Curitiba facility was built.
tfn.why: The text says consultation is needed but does not say whether it happened.

tfn.s: According to the writer, consent works differently for a medical treatment than for a mosquito release.
tfn.why: An individual may decline treatment, but nobody can opt out of the mosquitoes in their own street.

tfn.s: The writer treats the size of the Curitiba plant as a sign that a single release would be enough.
tfn.why: The text says a facility of this size admits the method only works "as a sustained operation, not as a one-off intervention".

focus.note: Some collocations are almost fixed chunks. You strike a balance, shed light on something and hold a vested interest. Learn the whole chunk.

speak.title: Role-play: a meeting about the mosquito release
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: Mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia will soon be released in a neighbourhood. Explain the plan to a resident. Answer at least two questions honestly, including the fact that the mosquitoes can still bite.

b.text: You live in the neighbourhood and you're worried about more mosquitoes near your home. Ask questions and say what would make you feel safer. Decide at the end if you support the plan.

phrases: I'm worried about the mosquitoes near my house.
I'd like to understand how it works.
Let me explain what we're doing.
They can still bite, but they don't pass on dengue as easily.
What if the plan doesn't work?
I'm still not convinced, but I'll come to the meeting.
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: did the resident support the plan, and what changed their mind?
